saint_pick.name: Agapius
saint_pick.selection_reason: Agapius has the best-documented story of the group: Eusebius, a near-contemporary eyewitness in Caesarea, records in The Martyrs of Palestine how he was condemned to the beasts in AD 306, offered a pardon, refused it, was mauled by a bear and survived, and was later drowned with weights tied to his feet. Strictly, the bear episode is a survival rather than a formally examined miracle, so it is a borderline fit for the miracle-led brief. The other candidates have thinner or legendary sources: Maurus of Parentium is the only one with a Nov 21 commemoration, but his story is mostly legend.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Martyr venerated in the Roman Martyrology (Latin Church); listed by Santi e Beati and Nominis as a saint of the Catholic Church. I am not certain of his exact calendar date, so check it before posting.

script.portrait: A Christian martyr of the early fourth century in a plain Roman-era tunic and mantle, standing and facing the viewer. He holds a martyr's palm, and a few stones lie at his feet. Behind him are the columns of a Roman harbor city and the blue Mediterranean.

beats.text: Offered his freedom, he refused it, and was given to a bear.
beats.scene: A Christian prisoner in a plain tunic stands alone on the sand of a Roman amphitheater, facing a brown bear. Tiers of stone seats rise behind him, and a robed official watches from a raised platform.

beats.text: Saint Agapius, fourth century, Caesarea, on the coast of modern Israel.
Persecution had come to the empire. More than once, Agapius was tortured, then held back for a greater trial.
beats.scene: A Christian prisoner sits in a dim Roman prison cell with a barred window, his hands bound. A guard stands at the arched door, and light falls across the stone floor.

beats.text: Eusebius, who lived near those years, tells it. In the amphitheater, before Maximinus, he was offered freedom if he renounced his faith. He refused.
beats.scene: A Christian prisoner stands before a Roman ruler seated on a raised throne in a crowded amphitheater. Soldiers flank the ruler, and the prisoner holds his head high with his hands open.

beats.text: According to tradition, the bear wounded him gravely, yet he still breathed. The next day, stones were tied to his feet, and he was drowned in the sea.
beats.scene: On a stone pier of a Roman harbor city, soldiers stand beside a wounded, quiet Christian prisoner with stones bound to his feet. The Mediterranean stretches out behind them under a pale sky.

beats.text: The account gives one reason for his refusal: faithfulness to the Creator. His courage pointed beyond him, to God alone. Faithfulness matters most when it costs the most.
beats.scene: A martyr in a plain tunic stands in light on a rocky shore, holding a palm. His face is turned upward to a golden sky, and a few stones lie at his feet.

claims.claim: Agapius was a martyr at Caesarea in Palestine in 306, in the early fourth century.
Caesarea Maritima was the seat of Roman provincial government on the Mediterranean coast; the persecutions began in the empire in 303.
Agapius had been tortured more than once but was always held back for greater trials.
His story is told by Eusebius of Caesarea, an author close to the events.
He was brought to the amphitheater in the presence of Maximinus Daia.
He was offered freedom if he abandoned the Christian faith and refused.
A bear was set on him in the arena; it wounded him gravely but he was still alive.
The next day stones were tied to his feet and he was drowned in the sea.
The reason Eusebius gives for his refusal is faithfulness to the Creator.
His feast in the Roman Martyrology is November 21.
Nothing certain is known of his birth, family or profession.
His emblem is the beast of the amphitheater and stones.
The Roman Martyrology states the bear and drowning according to tradition.
The name Agapios comes from the Greek agape, love.
Eusebius also records a different Agapius, beheaded at Caesarea with seven companions; the two must not be confused.
Eusebius's account survives in a short Greek version and a longer version preserved mostly in Syriac.
Nominis places the martyrdom during the persecutions of Diocletian and records the same sequence of bear and drowning.

story: Agapius is one of the martyrs of Palestine, remembered by the Church on November 21. His name comes from the Greek agape, which means love. Almost nothing is known about his early life. A Catholic reference says plainly that nothing certain is known of his birth, his family or his profession. What the Church remembers is how his life ended, in the city of Caesarea, in the year 306.

He lived in the age of the great persecution. In 303, under the rulers who then shared power in the Roman Empire, measures against Christians began to be enforced. In Palestine these measures changed from year to year and depended on provincial and imperial officials. Caesarea, on the Mediterranean coast, was the seat of the provincial government, and it saw trials, imprisonments and executions of Christians.

The record of these years was written by Eusebius, who later became bishop of the city. He gathered testimony about the Christians persecuted in the region. His work is not a Roman court register. It is a Christian work of memory, written by someone close to the events, and it is best read with care. It survives in a short Greek form and in a longer form preserved mostly in a Syriac version, which was published and translated in the nineteenth century by William Cureton. Both forms agree on the heart of Agapius's story. The longer version adds words attributed to him, but these cannot be treated as an exact transcript, so they are not repeated here.

According to Eusebius, Agapius had been tortured more than once, but each time he was held back for greater trials. At last he was brought to the amphitheater of Caesarea, in the presence of Maximinus Daia, who then held power in the eastern part of the empire. He was offered his freedom if he would give up the Christian faith. He refused. The reason Eusebius gives is not any crime, but faithfulness to his Creator.

A bear was then set upon him in the arena. It wounded him gravely, but he did not die at once. The Roman Martyrology, which tells this episode according to tradition, adds that because he was still breathing, he was drowned in the sea on the following day, with stones tied to his feet. His emblem in Christian art is the beast of the amphitheater and the stones. Where his body was laid is not known.

There is a second Agapius in Eusebius's pages, who was beheaded at Caesarea with seven companions, including two men named Alexander and two named Dionysius. He belongs to another episode of the persecution, and the two men should not be confused. Their stories do not agree, and nothing from one should be carried over to the other. The martyr of November 21 is the one linked with the bear and the sea.

The exact date has been understood in different ways. Eusebius places the event in November of the fourth year of the persecution. Some readers have placed the arena on November 20, with the drowning the next day, and some older martyrologies kept November 20. The Church today keeps his memory on November 21. The Church honors him as a saint in the Roman Martyrology, which recognizes his holiness. It does not claim more certainty than the sources allow.

That is a quiet legacy for a man whose life is otherwise hidden. Nothing certain is known of his work, and no words of his survive that can be trusted word for word. What remains is a refusal and the reason behind it. Offered his freedom, he chose faithfulness to God.

issues: Story beat 1: 'Again and again' overstates the sources, which say he was tortured 'more than once'. Changed to 'More than once'.

Story beat 3: the bear and the drowning were stated flatly. The Roman Martyrology gives them 'according to tradition', so the bear sentence now opens with 'According to tradition'. Total word count is now about 127.
Website story, paragraph 1: 'The Catholic references say plainly' rests on one Catholic reference (Santi e Beati), not several. Changed to 'A Catholic reference says'.

Website story, paragraph 8: 'no known office to boast of' is slightly irreverent and implies a fact the sources do not state. Wikipedia calls him a bishop, but the Catholic reference says nothing certain is known of his profession. Reworded to match the Catholic reference.

Checked and correct: the map point (Caesarea Maritima, 32.5, 34.9); the November 21 feast; 'Saint' and 'martyr' as titles; the Wikipedia-only details (bishop, arrested 304, August 19, 'rushed headlong') are correctly left out; the other Agapius, beheaded with seven companions, is kept separate; the hook is under 14 words and the who line under 15.
factcheck.reviewer_note: Please confirm you are comfortable with 'According to tradition' on the bear beat (the Roman Martyrology's wording), and note that Wikipedia's claim that he was a bishop was deliberately left out because the Catholic reference says nothing certain is known of his profession.

es.name: San Agapio
es.hook: Le ofrecieron la libertad delante de Maximino. Agapio dijo que no.
es.summary: Agapio, mártir de Cesarea a comienzos del siglo IV, se negó a renunciar a su fe a cambio de la libertad, sobrevivió a un oso en el anfiteatro y fue ahogado en el mar al día siguiente.
story: Agapio es uno de los mártires de Palestina, a quienes la Iglesia recuerda el 21 de noviembre. Su nombre procede del griego ágape, que significa amor. Se sabe casi nada de su vida temprana. Una referencia católica afirma con claridad que nada cierto se conoce sobre su nacimiento, su familia o su oficio. Lo que la Iglesia recuerda es cómo terminó su vida, en la ciudad de Cesarea, en el año 306.

Vivió en la época de la gran persecución. En el 303, bajo los gobernantes que entonces compartían el poder en el Imperio romano, comenzaron a aplicarse medidas contra los cristianos. En Palestina estas medidas cambiaban de un año a otro y dependían de los funcionarios provinciales e imperiales. Cesarea, en la costa del Mediterráneo, era la sede del gobierno provincial, y en ella hubo juicios, encarcelamientos y ejecuciones de cristianos.

El registro de estos años lo escribió Eusebio, que más tarde llegaría a ser obispo de la ciudad. Reunió testimonios sobre los cristianos perseguidos en la región. Su obra no es un registro de un tribunal romano. Es una obra cristiana de memoria, escrita por alguien cercano a los hechos, y conviene leerla con cuidado. Se conserva en una forma griega breve y en una forma más extensa, transmitida sobre todo en una versión siríaca, que fue publicada y traducida en el siglo XIX por William Cureton. Ambas formas coinciden en lo esencial de la historia de Agapio. La versión más larga añade palabras que se le atribuyen, pero no pueden tomarse como una transcripción exacta, así que no se repiten aquí.

Según Eusebio, Agapio había sido torturado más de una vez, pero en cada ocasión se le reservaba para pruebas mayores. Por fin fue llevado al anfiteatro de Cesarea, en presencia de Maximino Daya, quien entonces gobernaba la parte oriental del imperio. Se le ofreció la libertad si renunciaba a la fe cristiana. Se negó. La razón que da Eusebio no es ningún delito, sino la fidelidad a su Creador.

Entonces se soltó contra él un oso en la arena. Lo hirió gravemente, pero no murió de inmediato. El Martirologio Romano, que narra este episodio según la tradición, añade que, como todavía respiraba, fue ahogado en el mar al día siguiente, con piedras atadas a sus pies. Su emblema en el arte cristiano es la fiera del anfiteatro y las piedras. Se desconoce dónde fue depositado su cuerpo.

En las páginas de Eusebio aparece otro Agapio, que fue decapitado en Cesarea junto con siete compañeros, entre ellos dos hombres llamados Alejandro y dos llamados Dionisio. Pertenece a otro episodio de la persecución, y no deben confundirse los dos. Sus relatos no coinciden, y nada de uno debe trasladarse al otro. El mártir del 21 de noviembre es el vinculado con el oso y con el mar.

La fecha exacta se ha entendido de distintas maneras. Eusebio sitúa el suceso en noviembre del cuarto año de la persecución. Algunos lectores han ubicado el combate en el anfiteatro el 20 de noviembre, con el ahogamiento al día siguiente, y algunos martirologios antiguos conservaron el 20 de noviembre. Hoy la Iglesia celebra su memoria el 21 de noviembre. La Iglesia lo honra como santo en el Martirologio Romano, que reconoce su santidad. No reclama más certeza que la que permiten las fuentes.

Es un legado sereno para un hombre cuya vida, por lo demás, permanece oculta. Nada cierto se sabe de su obra, y no sobreviven palabras suyas que puedan tenerse por fidedignas literalmente. Lo que permanece es una negativa y la razón que la sostiene. Ofrecida la libertad, escogió la fidelidad a Dios.
